podcast.body: A song from the 1994 album "Ill Communication," which Mike D decided to write after the album was largely finished. It was released as a single four months before the album and is renowned for its Spike Jonze-directed video. The video, a parody of 1970s crime dramas, featured the band members in character with fake beards, a decision made due to Mike D's difficulty growing facial hair. "Sabotage from the Beastie Boys 1994 album, Ill Communication."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Beastie Boys' song "Sabotage" is highlighted as an example of music from the 1990s that helped to build momentum for Industrial Hip Hop, showcasing their distinctive blend of rap and rock. "Beastie Boy songs like Sabotage."

podcast.body: This brilliant song from the 1994 album *Ill Communication* was built around a bass line Adam Yauch was developing in rehearsals. Ad-Rock picked up a guitar and Mike D sat behind the drums to hash it out, with a working title of "Chris Rock" because a sound engineer named Chris thought the song "really rocked." The vocals were recorded on handheld mics to capture an authentic rap feel, and turntable scratches were later added. "The song itself was brilliant. Built around a bass line, Adam Yock was messing with in rehearsals."

podcast.body: This iconic song was released as a single four full months before its parent album, *Ill Communication*. The accompanying video, directed by former pro skateboarder Spike Jonze, famously featured the band members in fake hair and beards, a decision made because Mike D was "folically challenged" and couldn't grow facial hair for the shoot. "At first, everybody thought that this was a big risk, something that would make the video look cheesy, but in the end, the cheesiness made it work even better."
